html: Ukarãngmã is the name used by the Arara of Pará, a Carib-speaking people of the forests between the Xingu and Iriri rivers in the Brazilian Amazon. They avoided outsiders for most of the 1900s. The Trans-Amazonian Highway, cut through their land in the early 1970s, brought settlers and clashes, and government teams made peaceful contact with their groups between 1981 and 1987, when they numbered only a few hundred. The Belo Monte dam on the Xingu, built in the 2010s, added new pressure on their lands. Their neighbours include the Asurini in Brazil.
